topics: 🎯 Unwitting Like Intentional — five amoraic examples of temurah's unique stringency
🐐 Rabbi Elazar's List Revisited — kilayim, tereifa, tumtum: why they carry no inherent sanctity
🐕 Rava's Search for the Right Comparison — tereifa vs. a non-kosher animal vs. a blemished one
👪 New Mishna: Offspring and Substitutes of Peace Offerings, 'Until the End of the World'
📜 Deuteronomy 12:26-27 — must the substitute be sacrificed, or just kept alive?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing Chapter Two, Opening Chapter Three
overview.subtitle: Temurah 17a–17b
overview.hebrewSource: וְלַד שְׁלָמִים וּתְמוּרָתָן... עַד סוֹף כׇּל הָעוֹלָם — הֲרֵי הֵן שְׁלָמִים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf catalogs several amoraic examples of temurah's unique stringency — that an unwitting substitution is treated like an intentional one, incurring lashes, while unwitting consecration is not. It then returns to Rabbi Elazar's list of animals (hybrids, a tereifa, one born by caesarean, a tumtum, a hermaphrodite) that carry no inherent sanctity, with Rava working through several failed comparisons before settling on the right analogy to a non-kosher species. Chapter Two closes and Chapter Three opens with a new mishna: the offspring and substitutes of peace offerings retain peace-offering status through endless future generations — a rule the Gemara derives from a doubled 'male/female' in Leviticus 3:1, and from Deuteronomy 12:26-27's requirement that these animals actually be sacrificed, not merely kept until they die of neglect.

slides.title: 🎯 Five Ways 'Unwitting Equals Intentional' Only for Temurah
slides.subtitle: The Amoraim each supply a scenario testing Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's stringency
rows: Temurah: flogged and consecrated; ordinary consecration: not consecrated at all
Meant 'substitute for my burnt offering,' said 'peace offering'
Temurah takes effect; equivalent consecration error does not
Meant to name a black animal, said 'white' instead
The white animal becomes the (unintended) substitute; not so for consecration
Said 'let this leave, let that enter' (thinking this removes sanctity)
Liable for temurah; the parallel case of eating a blemished animal without redemption is not liable
Planned to act intentionally, but acted absentmindedly
Liable for temurah; not liable for the same slip with consecration

callout.label: Common thread:
callout.text: In every scenario, the same category of mental error that voids ordinary consecration still allows a substitution to fully take effect — the verse's extra 'shall be' (יִהְיֶה) covers even unwitting temurah.

slides.title: 🐐 Can These Animals Even Sanctify Something Else?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir presses Rabbi Elazar's ruling to its logical edge

lines.speaker: R' Elazar
lines.text: Kilayim, tereifa, yotzei dofen, tumtum, and androginos are neither sacred through consecration, nor can they sanctify a substitute.

lines.speaker: R' Meir
lines.text: But if they're never sacred to begin with, how could the ruling about substitutes even apply? You can't substitute FOR something that was never consecrated!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: It must mean: an animal consecrated WHILE fit, which only later became a tereifa or was born by caesarean after its mother's consecration — that's when the 'no substitute' half of the rule bites.

lines.speaker: For kilayim/tumtum/androginos
lines.text: These can only ever arise as the OFFSPRING of an already-consecrated animal (following Rabbi Yehuda, who holds offspring can generate temurah) — never through direct consecration.

callout.label: Shmuel's clarification:
callout.text: 'Neither sacred nor sanctify' means specifically: not sacred FOR PURPOSES OF SUBSTITUTION, and cannot GENERATE a substitute — not that they lack all sanctity whatsoever.

slides.title: 🐕 Rava's Search for the Right Comparison
slides.subtitle: Multiple attempts to explain why these animals lack inherent sanctity

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Pappa's first attempt: like a non-kosher animal — never sacrificed, never inherently sanctified
2️⃣ Challenge: but a BLEMISHED animal also can't be sacrificed, yet it DOES carry inherent sanctity! What's different?
3️⃣ Rava's 2nd attempt: a blemished animal's SPECIES is still sacrificed (unblemished ones); these categories never are — but then why does even a tereifa (whose species IS sacrificed) fail?

4️⃣ Rava's 3rd attempt: these are INHERENT disqualifications (like non-kosher status), unlike a blemish, which is merely a missing part — but wait, some listed blemishes (שָׂרוּעַ וְקָלוּט) are also inherent!
5️⃣ Final answer: compare to FOOD status — a non-kosher animal and a tereifa are both forbidden to EAT; a blemished animal remains permitted to eat. That distinction holds

callout.label: Method on display:
callout.text: Rava doesn't settle for the first plausible analogy — he tests it against every counter-example until one survives.

slides.title: 👪 New Mishna: Peace Offerings Propagate Forever
slides.subtitle: Unlike sin offerings, a peace offering's line never dies out

boxes.title: The Mishna's Rule
items: Offspring of a peace offering = a peace offering
Even THEIR offspring, and so on — 'until the end of all time' — remain peace offerings, requiring semikha, libations, and the waving of breast and thigh

boxes.title: Verse Source (Lev. 3:1)
items: Rav Safra questioned reversing this; Abaye defends the pairing by grammatical gender

callout.label: Why 'until the end of the world' is needed:
callout.text: The mishna anticipates Rabbi Elazar's later view (that a peace offering's direct offspring should NOT be sacrificed) and pointedly rejects it for every future generation, not just the first.

slides.title: 📜 Must the Substitute Actually Be Sacrificed?
slides.subtitle: Deuteronomy 12:26-27 settles the question — they aren't simply left to starve

nodes.content: ❓ 'רַק קָדָשֶׁיךָ אֲשֶׁר יִהְיוּ לָךְ... תִּשָּׂא וּבָאתָ' — bring substitutes ('your holy things') and offspring ('that you have') to the Temple. But then what — leave them to die of neglect?

📖 'וְעָשִׂיתָ עוֹלוֹתֶיךָ' — treat them the way you treat the offering they came from: a burnt-offering's substitute is sacrificed as a burnt offering; a peace-offering's is sacrificed as a peace offering

columns.label: R' Yishmael
columns.content: 'רַק' (only) limits this to SOME offerings, not all — a guilt offering's substitute, for instance, is excluded

columns.label: R' Akiva
columns.content: No limiting word is even needed — 'אָשָׁם הוּא' ('it is a guilt offering') already teaches: only IT is sacrificed, not its substitute

callout.label: Why this matters:
callout.text: Without this verse, one might assume all substitutes and offspring — even a sin offering's — must be brought to the Temple and starved there; the Torah instead directs that eligible ones (like a peace offering's) are actually sacrificed.

summary.principle: Temurah's unique stringency (unwitting equals intentional) is illustrated across many scenarios, animals with inherent disqualifications carry no sanctity at all, and — opening Chapter Three — a peace offering's line of offspring and substitutes remains sacrificial forever, actually sacrificed rather than merely kept alive.

flowSteps.content: 🎯 Five scenarios show: unwitting substitution still consecrates and incurs lashes; unwitting consecration does not
🐐 Rabbi Elazar's list: inherently disqualified animals carry no sanctity — refined through several failed analogies

columns.content: 👪 New mishna: peace offering's offspring/substitutes stay peace offerings forever
📜 Deut. 12:26-27: they must be sacrificed, not starved

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: only offerings the Torah specifically includes (like peace offerings) propagate sacrificial status through their line — others (like sin, guilt) do not

quiz.q: What is the common thread across the Amoraim's various examples of 'unwitting equals intentional' for temurah?
o: Unwitting substitution never takes effect
In every case, the same kind of mental error that would void ordinary consecration still allows the substitution to fully take effect and incur lashes
Only Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's own examples count
Unwitting acts are always exempt from lashes
quiz.e: Each scenario (Ḥizkiyya's, Reish Lakish/R' Yoḥanan's, Rav Sheshet's, etc.) shows that an unwitting act of substitution still consecrates the animal and incurs lashes, unlike the parallel case of unwitting consecration, which has no effect at all.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel's clarification of Rabbi Elazar's ruling, what does 'neither sacred nor sanctify' mean for animals like kilayim, tereifa, and tumtum?
o: They have absolutely no sanctity of any kind, ever
They cannot become a valid substitute, and cannot generate one either — not that they lack all sanctity in every sense
They may never be eaten
They are automatically considered non-sacred forever
quiz.e: Shmuel specifies the ruling is about temurah specifically: these animals cannot serve as, or generate, a substitute — leaving room for other forms of sanctity (like value-sanctity) to still apply.

quiz.q: In Rava's final, successful comparison, what distinguishes a tereifa and a non-kosher animal (no inherent sanctity) from a blemished animal (which DOES carry inherent sanctity)?
o: Their price
Both a non-kosher animal and a tereifa are forbidden to eat, while a blemished animal remains permitted to eat
Their color
Nothing distinguishes them
quiz.e: After several rejected comparisons, Rava settles on the food-status distinction: non-kosher animals and tereifot are forbidden for consumption, unlike a blemished (but still kosher) animal, which may still be eaten.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, how far does peace-offering status extend through a line of offspring and substitutes?
o: Only to the first generation of offspring
Only to the first substitute, not further
Indefinitely — 'until the end of all time' — every subsequent offspring or substitute remains a peace offering
It never applies to offspring, only substitutes
quiz.e: The mishna explicitly states that offspring, substitutes, and their offspring's offspring 'until the end of all time' all retain full peace-offering status, requiring semikha, libations, and the breast/thigh waving.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Akiva, what verse teaches that a guilt offering's (asham) substitute is NOT sacrificed on the altar?
o: 'רַק קָדָשֶׁיךָ' ('only your holy things')
'אָשָׁם הוּא' — 'it is a guilt offering' — the word 'הוּא' (it) implies only the original, not its substitute, is sacrificed
'זָכָר' ('male')
There is no such verse; Rabbi Akiva disagrees with the entire premise
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva derives from the emphatic 'הוּא' in 'it is a guilt offering' (Lev. 5:19) that only the guilt offering itself is sacrificed, excluding its substitute — making Rabbi Yishmael's broader limiting word 'רַק' unnecessary in his view.
